item.title: Alaskan Malamute: The Ultimate Guide to This Powerful Arctic Companion
item.dc:creator: RR
item.content:encoded:
In 2020, an Alaskan Malamute named Attla became the first of his breed to complete Australia's longest sled dog race — 200 kilometres through Victorian alpine terrain, proving that even in our sunburnt country, this Arctic powerhouse can thrive with the right care. That remarkable achievement tells you everything about what makes the Alaskan Malamute dog breed so special: unwavering endurance, fierce loyalty, and a work ethic that simply won't quit.

But here's what that headline doesn't tell you: the Alaskan Malamute isn't just any large, fluffy dog. They're living, breathing remnants of ancient history — one of the oldest Arctic sled breeds, originally developed by the Mahlemut Inuit people of Alaska thousands of years ago. Their strength-to-size ratio rivals professional athletes, and their pack mentality runs so deep it shapes every aspect of their behaviour.

If you're considering bringing one of these magnificent dogs into your life, you're in the right place. This guide covers everything from the realities of Alaskan Malamute shedding (spoiler: invest in a good vacuum) to the true costs of ownership in Australia in 2025.

What You'll Learn:

  • Breed traits & temperament
  • Health concerns to know
  • True cost in Australia (2025)
  • Training & exercise needs
  • Is this breed right for you?

Breed Quick Facts

Data sourced from ANKC Breed Standards and Dogs Australia registry.¹

History of the Alaskan Malamute

The Alaskan Malamute's story begins over 4,000 years ago with the Mahlemut Inuit tribe in northwestern Alaska. Unlike their Siberian Husky cousins — bred for speed — Malamutes were developed as freight dogs, capable of hauling heavy loads across vast frozen distances. Their name itself is a tribute to the Mahlemut people who perfected the breed.

According to the American Kennel Club's breed history archives, Malamutes played a crucial role in Admiral Byrd's Antarctic expeditions and served alongside Allied forces during World War II.² The breed nearly faced extinction in the early 20th century but was carefully preserved by dedicated breeders.

Alaskan Malamutes arrived in Australia in the 1970s, where breeders worked to establish the breed while adapting care practices for our warmer climate. Today, they remain relatively rare compared to their Husky counterparts, but dedicated Malamute communities thrive across the country, particularly in cooler regions like Tasmania, Victoria's highlands, and the Australian Alps.

Alaskan Malamute Temperament

Core Personality Traits

Loyal: Your Alaskan Malamute will follow you from room to room, supervising your every move with quiet dedication. This isn't clingy behaviour — it's an ancient pack instinct that makes you their entire world.

Independent: Don't mistake their devotion for obedience. Malamutes are intelligent problem-solvers who will question every command if they don't see the point. As one Victorian breeder put it: "A Malamute will sit when asked — but only after they've decided it was their idea first."

Affectionate: Beneath that imposing exterior lies a giant softie. Many Alaskan Malamute owners report that their dogs are surprisingly gentle, often trying to curl up in laps despite weighing over 40 kilograms.

Playful: Even into their senior years, Malamutes retain a puppy-like zest for life. Their idea of play often involves dramatic vocalisations — they're famous "talkers" rather than barkers.

Strong-Willed: This varies significantly between individual dogs — some Malamutes are eager to please while others have earned their reputation as the "stubborn ones" of the Arctic breeds.

Behaviour with Children

Alaskan Malamutes can be wonderful family dogs, but their size demands respect. They're generally patient with children and often become devoted protectors. However, their exuberance during play can accidentally knock over toddlers, so supervision is essential with children under eight.

First-time Alaskan Malamute owners are often surprised by how gentle these powerful dogs can be around small children — provided both dog and child are taught appropriate boundaries.

Behaviour with Other Pets

Here's where things get complicated. Malamutes have a strong prey drive inherited from their ancestors. While many coexist peacefully with cats they've been raised with, introducing new small pets later can be risky.

With other dogs, Malamutes often display same-sex aggression, particularly between males. Early socialisation is critical, but even well-socialised Malamutes may not tolerate unfamiliar dogs in their territory.

Common Behavioural Challenges

If your Alaskan Malamute starts digging craters in your backyard — and trust us, they will try — don't panic. This isn't destructive behaviour; it's an instinct to create cool resting spots. The solution? Provide a designated digging area filled with sand and redirect them there consistently.

Experienced Alaskan Malamute handlers often say that 90% of behavioural issues stem from insufficient exercise. A tired Malamute is a well-behaved Malamute; a bored one will redecorate your garden, reorganise your furniture, and possibly learn to open doors.

Alaskan Malamute Health Issues

If you're worried about your future Malamute's health, you're not alone — it's one of the first questions prospective owners ask. The good news is that with proper breeding, regular veterinary care, and appropriate exercise, many Alaskan Malamutes live long, healthy lives.

According to VCA Hospitals (vcahospitals.com), large breed dogs like Malamutes face specific health challenges that responsible owners should understand.³

Hip Dysplasia

Prevalence: Affects approximately 12-15% of the breed

Symptoms: Difficulty rising, reluctance to climb stairs, bunny-hopping gait, decreased activity

Treatment Cost (AUD): $1,500-$6,000 for surgery; $500-$1,500 for ongoing management

Prevention: Purchase from breeders who hip-score both parents; maintain healthy weight; avoid over-exercising puppies

Inherited Polyneuropathy (AMPN)

Prevalence: Rare but serious — affects the nervous system

Symptoms: Progressive weakness in hind legs, exercise intolerance, muscle wasting (typically appearing between 7-18 months)

Treatment Cost (AUD): No cure; supportive care $200-$500 annually

Prevention: DNA testing available — only purchase from breeders who test

Hypothyroidism

Prevalence: Common in middle-aged Malamutes

Symptoms: Weight gain despite normal eating, lethargy, coat dullness, skin problems

Treatment Cost (AUD): $300-$600 annually for lifelong medication

Prevention: Regular thyroid screening from age five

Bloat (Gastric Dilatation-Volvulus)

This can feel overwhelming at first, but understanding the signs can save your dog's life. Bloat is a medical emergency where the stomach twists, cutting off blood supply.

Symptoms: Distended abdomen, unproductive retching, restlessness, rapid breathing

Treatment Cost (AUD): $3,000-$10,000 for emergency surgery

Prevention: Feed multiple smaller meals, avoid exercise immediately after eating, use slow-feeder bowls

Lifespan & Longevity Tips

The average Alaskan Malamute lifespan is 10-14 years, which is respectable for a large breed. Veterinarians at the Australian Veterinary Association recommend the following to maximise your Malamute's years:⁴

  • Maintain ideal weight — obesity dramatically shortens large breed lifespans
  • Regular exercise — keeps joints healthy and prevents muscle wasting
  • Dental care — poor dental health affects overall longevity
  • Annual health screenings — early detection of breed-specific conditions
  • Mental stimulation — cognitive exercise is as important as physical

Many owners report that their Malamutes remain active and playful well into double digits when properly cared for.

Alaskan Malamute Grooming Guide

Let's address the elephant in the room: Alaskan Malamute shedding is legendary. These dogs "blow" their undercoat twice yearly, and during these periods, you'll wonder if you've adopted a dog or a fur-producing factory. But between blowouts, regular grooming keeps things manageable.

Grooming Schedule

Coat Colours and Types

The Alaskan Malamute coat comes in stunning variety: grey and white, black and white, red and white, sable and white, and occasionally all white (though pure white Alaskan Malamute dogs are less common). Their double coat provides remarkable insulation — keeping them warm in winter and surprisingly cool in summer if properly maintained.

Never shave a Malamute's coat! This destroys their natural temperature regulation and can cause permanent damage to coat texture.

Alaskan Malamute Exercise Needs

According to RSPCA Australia (rspca.org.au), large working breeds require substantial daily exercise for physical and mental wellbeing.⁵ For Malamutes, this isn't just a recommendation — it's essential for preventing behavioural disasters.

Daily Minimum: 90-120 minutes of exercise, ideally split into two sessions

Ideal Activities:

  • Long walks or hikes (they're incredible hiking companions)
  • Weight pulling (there are Australian clubs dedicated to this!)
  • Swimming (many Malamutes love water)
  • Running alongside a bicycle (once fully grown)
  • Interactive play sessions

When your Alaskan Malamute hits adolescence around 8-14 months, expect boundless energy that seems to defy physics. The key is to increase mental stimulation alongside physical exercise — puzzle feeders, scent work, and training sessions help drain that teenage energy constructively.

Many Alaskan Malamute owners report that the first year is the most challenging exercise-wise, but by age two, with consistent activity routines, you'll have the most dedicated adventure buddy imaginable.

Heat Considerations for Australia: Exercise your Malamute in early morning or evening during warmer months. Never exercise them in temperatures above 25°C. Provide constant access to shade and fresh water. Consider cooling mats and paddling pools.

Alaskan Malamute Training Guide

Don't be discouraged if your Alaskan Malamute seems to ignore basic commands initially — their independent thinking means they're processing whether compliance benefits them. With patience and high-value rewards, most owners see reliable obedience develop over time.

According to the American Kennel Club (akc.org), Arctic breeds like Malamutes respond best to positive reinforcement methods that respect their intelligence.⁶

Socialisation Timeline

Training Tips for Malamutes

If your Alaskan Malamute training sessions seem to go nowhere, this often indicates boredom rather than defiance. Try these adjustments:

  • Keep sessions short (10-15 minutes maximum)
  • Use extremely high-value treats (real meat, cheese)
  • Add variety — Malamutes hate repetition
  • End on success, even if it's something simple
  • Train before meals when motivation peaks

Experienced handlers often say that Malamute training is about negotiation rather than command. You're building a partnership with an intelligent creature who has opinions — respect that, and training becomes infinitely more rewarding.

Alaskan Malamute Price & Costs

Understanding the true Alaskan Malamute price in Australia helps you prepare financially and avoid backyard breeders offering suspiciously cheap puppies.

Where to Find Alaskan Malamutes

Find registered Alaskan Malamute breeders through the Dogs Australia Breeder Directory (dogsaustralia.org.au). Expect waitlists of 6-18 months for puppies from reputable breeders who health-test their dogs.

Consider adoption through PetRescue (petrescue.com.au) or contact Alaskan Malamute Rescue and Rehome Australia — adult Malamutes sometimes need new homes when families can't meet their exercise needs.

Initial Costs

Annual Ongoing Costs

  • Food: $1,200 - $2,000 (premium brands like Black Hawk, Ivory Coat)
  • Vet & Preventatives: $600 - $1,200 (check-ups, heartworm, flea/tick)
  • Pet Insurance: $800 - $1,500 (highly recommended)
  • Grooming: $400 - $720 (professional grooming 3-4 times yearly)
  • Miscellaneous: $300 - $600 (toys, treats, replacements)

TOTAL ANNUAL: $3,300 - $6,020

Lifetime Cost Estimate: $45,500 - $80,000 (based on 12-year lifespan, including initial costs and health emergencies)

Is an Alaskan Malamute Right for You?

Ideal Owner Profile

The perfect Alaskan Malamute owner is active, patient, and loves outdoor adventures. You have experience with large dogs (or are willing to learn intensively), enjoy regular exercise regardless of weather, and have the time for training and grooming commitments. You appreciate an independent spirit rather than instant obedience.

Living Requirements

Home Size: House with secure yard strongly preferred; apartment living is challenging but not impossible with extraordinary exercise commitment

Yard: Securely fenced (minimum 1.8 metres — Malamutes can jump) with shade

Climate: Cooler Australian climates ideal (Tasmania, Victoria, ACT). Can adapt to warmer areas with air conditioning and adjusted schedules

Who Should NOT Get a Malamute

This can feel overwhelming, but being honest about challenges upfront saves heartbreak later.

  • First-time dog owners seeking an easy breed
  • Sedentary households unable to provide 90+ minutes daily exercise
  • Those wanting off-leash reliability (prey drive makes this risky)
  • Households with small pets they weren't raised with
  • Anyone expecting low-maintenance companionship
  • People in very hot climates without air conditioning

Final Verdict: Is a Malamute Right for You?

Perfect for: Active individuals or families who love outdoor adventures, have large secure properties, appreciate independent-minded dogs, and are prepared for serious grooming commitments.

Think twice if: You're seeking your first dog, work long hours, have limited outdoor space, live in tropical Australia without climate control, or want a dog who follows commands without question.

First-time owner rating: Challenging but not impossible. If you're determined, find an experienced mentor, enrol in training classes before your puppy arrives, and be prepared to learn as you go.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Are Alaskan Malamutes good for first-time owners?

A: While not the easiest breed for beginners, dedicated first-time owners can succeed with proper preparation, professional training support, and realistic expectations.¹

Q: Do Alaskan Malamutes shed a lot?

A: Yes — Alaskan Malamute shedding is significant. They blow their undercoat twice yearly and shed moderately year-round. Regular brushing minimises loose fur.

Q: How much exercise does an Alaskan Malamute need?

A: Adults require 90-120 minutes of daily exercise, including both physical activity and mental stimulation.

Q: How long do Alaskan Malamutes live?

A: The average Alaskan Malamute lifespan is 10-14 years with proper nutrition, exercise, and healthcare.

Q: How much does an Alaskan Malamute cost in Australia?

A: Expect $2,500-$5,000 for a registered puppy. Adoption fees range $350-$700. Annual costs average $3,300-$6,020.

Q: Are Alaskan Malamutes good with children?

A: Generally yes — they're patient and protective. Their size means supervision is essential with young children.

Q: Are Alaskan Malamutes aggressive?

A: Not inherently toward humans, but may display same-sex dog aggression and have strong prey drive toward small animals.

Q: Can an Alaskan Malamute live in hot weather?

A: Yes, with careful management: air conditioning, early/evening exercise only, constant water, and never exercising above 25°C.

Australian Cobberdog: The Ultimate Guide to This Purpose-Bred Companion

In 2012, after decades of careful development, a new breed quietly entered the world's registry books — the Australian Cobberdog. While most people have heard of the Labradoodle, far fewer know about its purpose-bred descendant, a dog specifically developed to be the ultimate therapy and assistance companion. The name itself tells you everything: 'Cobber' is Australian slang for mate, friend, the one you can count on.

So what is a Cobberdog, exactly? Unlike the Labradoodle — which became so popular that breeding standards collapsed — the Australian Cobberdog represents a return to the original vision: a hypoallergenic, non-shedding dog with an intuitive, gentle temperament ideally suited for families and therapeutic work. If you've been searching for an intelligent, empathetic companion that won't trigger allergies, you're in the right place.

What You'll Learn:

  • Breed traits & temperament
  • Health concerns to know
  • True cost in Australia (2025)
  • Training & exercise needs
  • Is this breed right for you?

Cobberdog Quick Facts

Data sourced from MDBA Breed Standards and registered Australian breeders.¹

History of the Cobberdog

The Australian Cobberdog story begins with Wally Conron, who in the 1980s created the first intentional Labrador-Poodle cross while working as a puppy-breeding manager for the Royal Guide Dogs Association of Australia. His goal was simple but revolutionary: create a hypoallergenic guide dog for a blind woman whose husband had severe allergies.²

The concept worked, but success brought problems. As 'Labradoodles' exploded in popularity, unscrupulous breeders began crossing any Labrador with any Poodle and selling the puppies at premium prices — with no regard for temperament, health, or whether they were actually hypoallergenic. The original vision was lost in a flood of inconsistent dogs.

Enter Beverley Rutland-Manners and her daughter Mellodie Woolley of Rutland Manor and Tegan Park breeding centres. Determined to restore the original purpose, they developed a careful breeding programme using multiple breeds — not just Labradors and Poodles — to achieve consistent temperament, coat type, and health. In 2012, after submitting detailed records to the Master Dog Breeders and Associates (MDBA), the Australian Cobberdog was officially recognised as a pure breed in development with its own unique DNA sequence.

The difference between a Cobberdog and Labradoodle is fundamental: while a Labradoodle can be any Poodle-Labrador cross with unpredictable results, an Australian Cobberdog comes with a pedigree, breed standard, and the assurance of carefully selected genetics. Only MDBA-registered breeders can issue authentic Cobberdog pedigrees.

Australian Cobberdog Temperament

The Australian Cobberdog temperament is, quite simply, what sets this breed apart from all others. These dogs were specifically developed to excel in therapy and assistance work — and that breeding shines through in every interaction.

Core Personality Traits

Intuitive: Many Cobberdog owners report that their dogs seem to 'read' human emotions. They naturally seek eye contact — not in a demanding way, but with a quiet understanding that can feel almost uncanny. This trait makes them exceptional therapy dogs for people with anxiety, autism, or PTSD.

Gentle: The breed standard specifically states that Australian Cobberdogs should be 'totally non-aggressive.' This isn't just marketing — it's bred into their DNA. As one Queensland breeder put it: 'A Cobberdog would rather lick an intruder to death than bark at them.'

Intelligent: Descended from some of the smartest working breeds, Cobberdogs pick up commands with remarkable speed. First-time Cobberdog owners are often surprised by how quickly their puppy learns — show them something once, and they've got it.

Joyful: There's a reason Cobberdogs are often described as 'goofy.' They have an infectious enthusiasm for life and genuinely seem to enjoy making their humans laugh. This varies between individual dogs, but the comical streak is a breed hallmark.

Loyal: While friendly to everyone, Cobberdogs form deep bonds with their families. They want to be wherever you are — not underfoot demanding attention, but quietly nearby, ready to offer comfort or companionship.

Behaviour with Children

Australian Cobberdogs excel with children of all ages. Their gentle, patient nature and lack of aggression makes them ideal family companions. Breeders consistently note that Cobberdogs seem to have a special affinity for children, often becoming their devoted shadows and playmates. As always, supervise interactions with young children and teach kids appropriate handling.

Behaviour with Other Pets

The breed has a moderate prey drive, meaning they generally coexist well with cats and other household pets, especially when introduced properly. Their sociable nature extends to other dogs — most Cobberdogs love canine companionship and play well at dog parks.

Common Behavioural Challenges

If your Cobberdog starts following you from room to room, becoming anxious when left alone, or getting into mischief — don't panic. This is often separation anxiety, and it's the flip side of their strong bonding instinct. According to owners in Australian Cobberdog communities, this is one of the most common challenges new owners face. The solution? Gradual alone-time training from puppyhood, ensuring they have mental stimulation when you're away, and never making departures or arrivals overly emotional.

Cobberdog Health Issues

If you're worried about potential health problems with this breed, you're not alone — and asking these questions upfront is exactly right. The good news is that responsible Cobberdog breeding specifically prioritises health, with mandatory DNA testing requirements that many other breeds lack.

According to VCA Hospitals, hip dysplasia — a common concern in medium to large breeds — can affect dogs when the hip socket doesn't properly cover the ball portion of the thigh bone.³ The MDBA requires hip and elbow scoring for all breeding dogs to minimise this risk in Cobberdog lines.

Hip and Elbow Dysplasia

  • Risk Level: Low to moderate with properly tested parents
  • Symptoms: Lameness, difficulty rising, reluctance to exercise
  • Treatment Cost (AUD): $3,000-$7,000 per joint if surgery required
  • Prevention: Choose MDBA-registered breeders with hip scores; maintain healthy weight; avoid excessive exercise during growth

Progressive Retinal Atrophy (PRA-prcd)

An inherited eye condition that can cause blindness.⁴ DNA testing can identify carriers and affected dogs, allowing responsible breeders to ensure no puppies are at risk. Always ask to see PRA test results for both parents.

Other Conditions to Discuss with Breeders

  • Degenerative Myelopathy (spinal cord disease)
  • Exercise Induced Collapse
  • Von Willebrand Disease (bleeding disorder)
  • Addison's Disease

The MDBA mandates DNA testing for approximately 30 hereditary conditions before breeding dogs can be registered. This is one of the most comprehensive testing requirements of any breed — and a major reason why health-conscious families choose Cobberdogs over less regulated alternatives.

Lifespan & Longevity Tips

The Australian Cobberdog has an expected lifespan of 12-15 years, with a healthspan target of 16 years according to the MDBA.⁵ This is above average for dogs of their size, reflecting the breed's focus on genetic health.

Veterinarians at the Australian Veterinary Association recommend the following for maximising your Cobberdog's lifespan:⁶

  • Annual vet check-ups (twice yearly for dogs over 7)
  • Maintaining a lean body weight (Cobberdogs should look slender when wet)
  • Regular dental care — this breed can be prone to early plaque buildup
  • Quality nutrition appropriate for life stage
  • Protecting joints during the growth period (see Exercise section)

Cobberdog Grooming Guide

The non-shedding, hypoallergenic coat is one of the Cobberdog's biggest selling points — but it comes with a trade-off. That beautiful fleece or wool coat requires regular maintenance to prevent matting and keep your dog comfortable.

Coat Types: Cobberdogs come in three coat textures: straight fleece (gentle waves), wavy fleece, and curly fleece. Curlier coats require more frequent brushing to prevent matting. All coat types are non-shedding when properly bred.

Important: Don't skip paw pad hair trimming — long hair between the pads can cause slipping on hard floors and lead to joint strain. Trim every few weeks.

Cobberdog Exercise Needs

The RSPCA Australia recommends that companion dogs receive regular daily exercise for both physical and mental wellbeing.⁷ For Australian Cobberdogs, this typically means 30-60 minutes of activity per day, though this varies by size and individual energy level.

Experienced Cobberdog handlers often say that mental exercise is just as important as physical exercise for this intelligent breed. A 20-minute training session can tire them out as effectively as a 40-minute walk. Interactive games, puzzle feeders, and nose work are excellent supplements to daily walks.

Critical for Puppies and Young Dogs: If you notice your puppy limping, bunny-hopping, or reluctant to exercise, this often indicates joint stress that could lead to long-term problems. Cobberdogs' skeletal growth isn't complete until 18-24 months. During this period, avoid stairs, jumping onto beds or cars, forced running, and excessive ball-throwing. Let them set their own pace.

Swimming: Most Cobberdogs love water, and swimming is excellent low-impact exercise that builds muscle without stressing joints. It's particularly beneficial during the growth phase and for senior dogs.

Cobberdog Training Guide

Don't be discouraged if your Cobberdog puppy seems to learn too quickly — and then starts testing boundaries. Their intelligence sometimes means they're several steps ahead of you, figuring out which rules they can bend.

Australian Cobberdogs are renowned for their trainability. Their eagerness to please combined with high intelligence makes them star pupils in obedience classes. Professional dog trainers recommend starting training immediately upon bringing your puppy home — they're ready to learn from day one.⁸

When your Cobberdog hits adolescence around 6-10 months, expect some regression and selective hearing. The key is patience and consistency — this phase is temporary. Cobberdogs mature into remarkably well-behaved adults when given proper guidance during puppyhood.

Australian Cobberdog Price

Understanding the true cost of Cobberdog ownership helps you budget appropriately and recognise red flags. According to PetSure's annual pet ownership data, medium to large companion breeds like the Cobberdog typically represent a significant lifetime investment.⁹

Initial Costs

Annual Ongoing Costs

  • Food (premium quality): $800 - $1,200
  • Vet & Preventatives: $400 - $800
  • Pet Insurance: $500 - $1,000
  • Professional Grooming: $600 - $1,200 (every 6-8 weeks)
  • TOTAL ANNUAL: $2,300 - $4,200

Lifetime Cost Estimate: $35,000 - $60,000 (based on 13-year average lifespan)

Finding Your Australian Cobberdog

Find MDBA-registered breeders through the Master Dog Breeders and Associates directory. Verify any breeder's MDBA membership number before purchasing — if a breeder can't provide this, they cannot guarantee their dogs are authentic Australian Cobberdogs.

Red Flags: Be wary of prices significantly below $4,000 AUD, breeders who won't show health testing results, multiple litters available immediately, or anyone selling 'Cobberdogs' without MDBA registration.

Consider adoption through PetRescue (petrescue.com.au). While purebred Cobberdogs rarely appear in rescue, Labradoodles and Labradoodle mixes frequently do — and may suit families who don't require the predictability of MDBA breeding standards.

Is a Cobberdog Right for You?

Ideal Owner Profile: The Australian Cobberdog suits families, individuals, couples, and seniors who want an engaged, affectionate companion. They thrive with owners who can provide regular companionship, mental stimulation, and commit to the grooming requirements of their non-shedding coat.

Living Requirements

  • Home Size: Adaptable — miniature Cobberdogs suit apartments; medium and standard do best with a yard
  • Yard: Beneficial but not essential with adequate daily exercise
  • Climate: Adaptable to Australian conditions; provide shade and cooling in summer

Who Should NOT Get a Cobberdog

This can feel overwhelming, but being honest about challenges upfront saves heartbreak later.

  • Those who work long hours and cannot provide companionship — Cobberdogs are prone to separation anxiety
  • Anyone unwilling to commit to regular grooming — their coat requires consistent maintenance
  • Families seeking a guard dog — Cobberdogs are friendly to everyone and non-aggressive by design
  • Those on a tight budget — between purchase price and ongoing grooming, Cobberdogs are not an inexpensive breed

Final Verdict: Is a Cobberdog Right for You?

Perfect for: Families with allergy sufferers, those seeking therapy or assistance dogs, first-time owners who want an intelligent and forgiving companion, and anyone who values a deep emotional bond with their pet.

Think twice if: You need a guard dog, work extremely long hours away from home, dislike grooming maintenance, or are looking for a budget-friendly breed.

First-time owner rating: Ideal choice. The Australian Cobberdog's gentle nature, exceptional trainability, and intuitive understanding of human emotions make them one of the best breeds for first-time dog owners who want a companion that's loving, intelligent, and genuinely wants to make you happy.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: What is an Australian Cobberdog?

A: An Australian Cobberdog is a purebred dog in development, descended from the original Australian Labradoodle but with additional breeds carefully introduced to achieve consistent temperament and hypoallergenic coats. Unlike Labradoodles, Cobberdogs are registered with the MDBA and bred to strict standards.

Q: What is the difference between a Cobberdog and a Labradoodle?

A: A Labradoodle is any cross between a Labrador and Poodle, with unpredictable results. An Australian Cobberdog has a verified pedigree, undergoes mandatory health testing, and meets breed standards for temperament and coat type. Cobberdogs are reliably hypoallergenic; Labradoodles often are not.¹⁰

Q: Are Australian Cobberdogs hypoallergenic?

A: Yes, when properly bred from MDBA-registered parents, Australian Cobberdogs have non-shedding, allergy-friendly coats. However, some people may still react to dog saliva. If allergies are your primary concern, spend time with adult Cobberdogs before committing.

Q: Do Cobberdogs shed?

A: Authentic Australian Cobberdogs do not shed. Their fleece or wool coat grows continuously like human hair, which is why regular grooming and clipping is essential.

Q: How much does an Australian Cobberdog cost in Australia?

A: Expect to pay $4,500-$6,000 AUD from an MDBA-registered breeder. Prices significantly below this range should raise questions about authenticity and breeding standards.

Q: What sizes do Cobberdogs come in?

A: Cobberdogs come in three official sizes: Miniature (33-43 cm), Medium (43-50 cm), and Standard (53-60 cm). The mini Australian Cobberdog is popular for apartment living, while standard Cobberdogs suit families with more space.

Q: How long do Australian Cobberdogs live?

A: The average lifespan is 12-15 years, with a healthspan target of 16 years. This is above average for dogs of their size, reflecting the breed's focus on genetic health.

Sources & References

1. Master Dog Breeders and Associates (MDBA) — Official breed registry and standards

2. Rutland Manor & Tegan Park — Breed founder documentation

Veterinary & Health Sources:

3. VCA Hospitals — Hip dysplasia in dogs

4. Orthopedic Foundation for Animals (OFA) — PRA testing data

5. MDBA Breed Standard — Healthspan targets

6. Australian Veterinary Association — Preventative care guidelines

7. RSPCA Australia — Exercise requirements for companion dogs

8. Professional dog trainers — Positive reinforcement methods

9. PetSure (Bow Wow Meow) — Australian pet ownership cost data

10. MDBA Breed Comparison — Cobberdog vs Labradoodle distinction

item.content:encoded:
Despite their name suggesting an outback origin, the Australian Shepherd was actually developed in the western United States during the 19th century. This surprising fact hints at the breed's complex history — and if you're considering bringing one of these stunning dogs into your life, understanding their true nature is just as important as appreciating their striking blue eyes and merle coats.

The Australian Shepherd consistently ranks among the most intelligent dog breeds worldwide, and in Australian homes, they've become beloved companions for active families, rural property owners, and dog sport enthusiasts alike.¹ But make no mistake — this breed's exceptional intelligence comes with exceptional demands. Your Australian Shepherd won't be content lounging on the couch while you binge-watch television.

What You'll Learn

  • Breed traits & temperament
  • Health concerns to know
  • True cost in Australia
  • Training & exercise needs
  • Is this breed right for you?

Breed Quick Facts Table

History of the Australian Kelpie

The Australian Shepherd's name is something of a misnomer. According to the American Kennel Club's breed history archives, these dogs actually originated in the Pyrenees Mountains between Spain and France, where Basque shepherds bred them for herding livestock.² When these shepherds emigrated to Australia in the early 1800s, and later to California during the Gold Rush era, their dogs came along — and Americans assumed the 'exotic' herding dogs had Australian origins.

In the United States, ranchers refined the breed specifically for the demands of American ranching, creating a versatile working dog capable of managing cattle, sheep, and even protecting property. The breed gained enormous popularity through rodeo performances and Western films throughout the mid-20th century.

Australian Shepherds arrived in Australia during the late 20th century and quickly found a niche among rural property owners and dog sport competitors. Today, they're recognised by Dogs Australia and are particularly popular in Queensland, New South Wales, and Victoria, where their weather tolerance and work ethic suit both farm life and suburban activity.

Australian Shepherd Temperament

Loyal? Absolutely. Your Australian Shepherd will follow you from room to room, supervising your every move with quiet dedication. But don't mistake their devotion for low maintenance — this breed demands serious mental and physical engagement.

  • Intelligence: Ranked among the top 10 most intelligent breeds, Aussies learn commands rapidly — sometimes too rapidly. Many Australian Shepherd owners report that their dogs figured out how to open doors, gates, and even refrigerators within the first year.
  • Loyalty: Deeply bonded to their families, often choosing a 'favourite person' while remaining affectionate with everyone.
  • Energy: High-drive dogs bred for all-day work. Your Aussie won't be satisfied with a casual stroll around the block.
  • Alertness: Natural watchdogs who notice everything — which can tip into reactivity without proper socialisation.
  • Playfulness: Maintains puppy-like enthusiasm well into adulthood, delighting in games, tricks, and interactive play.

Australian Shepherds can be wonderful family dogs, though their herding instincts require management. Every Australian Shepherd is different, but the general tendency is to view small, fast-moving children as 'livestock' that needs organising. Supervision is essential with children under eight, and you'll need to teach both your dog and your children appropriate boundaries.

With proper introduction and socialisation, Aussies generally coexist well with other dogs. Cats and small animals are another matter — your experience may differ, particularly if your Aussie has a strong prey drive or wasn't raised alongside cats from puppyhood. First-time Australian Shepherd owners are often surprised by how intensely their dog watches the family cat's every movement.

If your Australian Shepherd starts nipping at heels or circling family members, don't panic — this is herding behaviour, not aggression. Redirect that energy immediately with a game of fetch or a training session. As one Queensland breeder put it: 'A bored Aussie is a creative Aussie — and their creativity usually involves reorganising your furniture, excavating your garden, or teaching themselves to open cupboards.'

Experienced Australian Shepherd handlers often say that the breed's biggest challenge isn't physical energy — it's mental energy. A physically tired Aussie who hasn't been mentally challenged will still find ways to entertain themselves, often destructively.

Australian Shepherd Health Issues

If you're worried about health issues in Australian Shepherds, you're not alone — it's one of the first things prospective owners ask. The good news is that with responsible breeding and proactive veterinary care, most Aussies live long, healthy lives.

According to VCA Hospitals, the following conditions are most common in Australian Shepherds:³

Prevalence: Approximately 6-8% of Australian Shepherds

Symptoms: Difficulty rising, reluctance to jump or climb stairs, bunny-hopping gait

Treatment Cost (AUD): $3,000-$8,000 for surgery; $500-$1,500/year for management

Prevention: Choose breeders who hip-score parents; maintain healthy weight; avoid over-exercising puppies

This genetic mutation affects how your dog processes certain medications. According to veterinary research, approximately 50% of Australian Shepherds carry at least one copy of the MDR1 mutation.⁴ Dogs with this mutation can have severe, potentially fatal reactions to common medications including ivermectin (found in some heartworm preventatives), loperamide (Imodium), and certain sedatives. A simple DNA test can identify carriers — ask your vet or breeder about testing.

Progressive Retinal Atrophy (PRA): Gradual vision loss; genetic testing available

Cataracts: Can develop at any age; surgery costs $3,000-$5,000 per eye

Collie Eye Anomaly (CEA): Present from birth; severity varies widely

Idiopathic epilepsy occurs in approximately 2-4% of Australian Shepherds.⁵ While witnessing a seizure is frightening, most dogs with epilepsy can be well-managed with medication costing $50-$150 monthly. If you notice your dog experiencing seizures, your vet can develop a management plan tailored to your dog's needs.​

Australian Shepherd Lifespan & Longevity Tips

The average Australian Shepherd lifespan is 12-15 years, with many individuals reaching their mid-teens when well cared for. Veterinarians at the Australian Veterinary Association recommend the following for maximising your Aussie's healthy years:⁶

  • Maintain a healthy weight — obesity significantly shortens lifespan
  • Schedule annual vet check-ups (twice yearly for dogs over 7)
  • Keep up with dental care — dental disease affects overall health
  • Provide appropriate exercise without over-stressing joints
  • Feed a high-quality, age-appropriate diet

Australian Shepherd Grooming Guide

That beautiful double coat requires commitment. Australian Shepherds shed moderately year-round and heavily ('blow coat') twice yearly during seasonal changes. If you're imagining a pristine, fur-free home, this isn't your breed.

Grooming Schedule Table

Important: Never shave your Australian Shepherd's double coat. The undercoat provides insulation from both heat and cold, and shaving can permanently damage coat texture and regrowth patterns. For dental care, products like Greenies or Oravet chews (available at most Australian pet stores and vet clinics) help maintain oral health between professional cleanings.

Australian Shepherds come in four recognised colours: black, blue merle, red, and red merle — each potentially with white markings and/or copper points. The striking merle pattern results from a gene that creates mottled patches of colour, often accompanied by blue or heterochromatic eyes.

Australian Shepherd Exercise

The RSPCA Australia recommends that active breeds like Australian Shepherds receive a minimum of 90-120 minutes of exercise daily.⁷ But here's what those numbers don't tell you: not all exercise is created equal for this breed.

Breeders consistently note that Australian Shepherds need mental exercise as much as physical activity. A 30-minute training session or puzzle-solving game can tire your Aussie out more effectively than an hour of walking. According to owners in Australian Shepherd communities, the most successful exercise routines combine physical activity with mental challenges: agility training, herding trials, nose work, or advanced obedience.

If your Aussie hits adolescence around 8-14 months and suddenly seems to have boundless, uncontrollable energy, don't panic. This is completely normal. The key is to increase mental stimulation alongside physical exercise — add training challenges, rotate puzzle toys, and consider structured activities like flyball or dock diving.

Warning signs of under-exercised Aussies: excessive barking, destructive chewing, digging, pacing, hyperactivity indoors, and attempts to 'herd' family members or other pets.

Australian Shepherd Training Tips

Don't be discouraged if your Australian Shepherd seems to learn commands instantly but then 'forgets' them in new environments — this is normal for intelligent dogs who need extensive generalisation training. The good news is that Aussies are incredibly responsive to positive reinforcement, and most owners see remarkable progress by the six-month mark.

Professional dog trainers recommend starting structured training from the day you bring your Australian Shepherd home. These dogs thrive on having a 'job,' and training provides exactly that mental engagement they crave. The American Kennel Club's training resources emphasise early socialisation as critical for this breed.⁸

Socialisation & Training Timeline

Training tip: If you notice your Aussie becoming 'stubborn' or disengaged, they're likely bored. Switch up your training approach, introduce new challenges, or take a break. These dogs are eager to please but need variety to stay interested.

Australian Shepherd Price & Costs

Understanding the true cost of Australian Shepherd ownership helps you budget realistically. Pet insurance companies like PetSure and Bow Wow Meow provide Australian-specific cost data that's invaluable for planning.⁹

Where to Find Your Australian Shepherd

Find registered breeders through the Dogs Australia Breeder Directory. Consider adoption through PetRescue or breed-specific rescues like Australian Shepherd Rescue Australia.

Initial Costs:

Annual Ongoing Costs:

  • Food (premium quality like Black Hawk or Ivory Coat): $1,200 - $1,800
  • Vet & Preventatives: $500 - $800
  • Pet Insurance: $600 - $1,200
  • Grooming: $400 - $800
  • TOTAL ANNUAL: $2,700 - $4,600

Lifetime Cost Estimate: $38,000 - $65,000 (based on 13-year average lifespan).

Is an Australian Shepherd Right for You?

Active individuals or families who can provide 90+ minutes of daily exercise, enjoy training and mental enrichment activities, and have time to dedicate to a highly bonded, velcro-style companion. Australian Shepherds thrive with owners who want a dog that participates in their daily lives, whether that's farm work, hiking, dog sports, or active family activities.

  • Home Size: House with yard strongly preferred; apartments possible only with extensive daily exercise commitment
  • Yard: Secure fencing essential — Aussies are athletic and can clear low barriers
  • Climate: Adaptable to most Australian climates; avoid strenuous exercise during extreme heat

This can feel overwhelming, but being honest about challenges upfront saves heartbreak later.

  • Those working long hours with limited time for exercise and training
  • People seeking a low-maintenance, couch-potato companion
  • First-time owners unwilling to invest in professional training or puppy classes
  • Those intolerant of heavy shedding and regular grooming requirements
  • Apartment dwellers without dedicated time for daily off-property exercise

The Australian Shepherd is a remarkable breed — intelligent, loyal, athletic, and endlessly devoted to their families. But that devotion comes with demands that not every owner can meet.

First-time owner rating: Challenging but achievable with commitment to training classes and daily engagement

Perfect for: Active families, rural property owners, dog sport enthusiasts, and dedicated owners wanting a trainable, velcro companion

Think twice if: You work long hours, prefer low-maintenance pets, or can't commit to extensive daily exercise and mental stimulation

Australian Shepherds FAQs

Are Australian Shepherds good for first-time owners?

Australian Shepherds can work for dedicated first-time owners, but they're not the easiest choice. Their high intelligence and energy require consistent training, extensive exercise, and mental enrichment. If you're willing to invest in puppy classes, commit to daily activity, and learn positive reinforcement techniques, you can succeed — but be prepared for a steep learning curve.¹⁰

Do Australian Shepherds shed a lot?

Yes. Australian Shepherds shed moderately year-round and heavily twice yearly during seasonal coat changes. Regular brushing (2-3 times weekly, daily during shedding seasons) helps manage fur, but expect to find hair on your furniture, clothing, and floors.

How much exercise does an Australian Shepherd need?

A minimum of 90-120 minutes daily, combining physical activity with mental stimulation. Simple walks aren't enough — Australian Shepherds need running, playing, training sessions, and puzzle-solving to stay balanced and happy.

How long do Australian Shepherds live?

The average Australian Shepherd lifespan is 12-15 years. With proper care, many Aussies reach their mid-teens. Regular veterinary care, appropriate exercise, dental care, and maintaining a healthy weight all contribute to longevity.

How much does an Australian Shepherd cost in Australia?

Expect to pay $2,500-$4,500 for a registered Australian Shepherd puppy from a reputable breeder in 2025. Adoption fees typically range from $350-$600. Annual ongoing costs run $2,700-$4,600 for food, veterinary care, insurance, and grooming.

Are Australian Shepherds good with children?

Australian Shepherds can be excellent family dogs when properly trained and supervised. However, their herding instincts may lead them to nip at or 'herd' small children who run or scream. Supervision is essential with young children, and both the dog and children need to be taught appropriate interactions.

item.title: Brittany Spaniel: The Versatile Sporting Dog
item.dc:creator: RR
item.content:encoded:
There's a reason the Brittany Spaniel consistently ranks among the top pointing breeds in field trial competitions worldwide — pound for pound, this compact sporting dog delivers more versatility, athleticism, and heart than breeds twice their size. Originally bred to work closely with hunters in the rugged Brittany region of France, these dogs have an almost uncanny ability to read their handler's intentions.

Despite being called a "spaniel," the Brittany actually works more like a pointer or setter, ranging ahead to locate game birds before freezing in that iconic pointing stance. In 1982, the American Kennel Club officially dropped "Spaniel" from the breed name, though Australians and many other countries still affectionately use the full title.

What makes the breed truly special isn't just their hunting prowess — it's their remarkable ability to transition from tireless field companion to devoted family pet. If you're considering this energetic, affectionate breed, you're in for an adventure that combines the best of sporting dog athleticism with genuine household companionship.

What You'll Learn

  • Breed traits & temperament
  • Health concerns to know
  • True cost in Australia
  • Training & exercise needs
  • Is this breed right for you?

Breed Quick Facts Table

Breed History & Origins

The Brittany Spaniel emerged from the forested, hilly terrain of northwestern France during the 17th and 18th centuries. Local hunters needed a versatile dog that could point, flush, and retrieve game across challenging landscapes — and do it all day without tiring. The breed developed from crosses between local French spaniels and English pointing dogs brought over by visiting hunters.²

What set Brittany apart was their compact size combined with tireless stamina. Unlike larger pointing breeds, Brittanys could work thick cover and navigate dense undergrowth while still covering impressive ground. French peasant hunters prized them because they didn't require horses to keep up with — a practical consideration that shaped the breed's moderate size.

Brittany arrived in Australia during the mid-20th century, finding a natural home among bird hunters and field trial enthusiasts. According to Dogs Australia, the breed has maintained a dedicated following, particularly in rural areas where their hunting abilities remain highly valued.³ Today, they're increasingly popular as active family companions in suburban homes across the country.

Temperament & Personality

Many Brittany Spaniel owners report that living with this breed feels like having a perpetually enthusiastic teammate who's always ready for the next adventure — whether that's a bushwalk, a backyard game, or simply following you from room to room.

Eager to Please: The breed temperament centres on a genuine desire to make their people happy. This trait makes them highly trainable and responsive, though it also means they're sensitive to harsh corrections.

Energetic: This isn't a breed content with lounging on the couch all day. they possess seemingly endless reserves of energy that need appropriate outlets through exercise and mental stimulation.

Affectionate: These dogs form deep bonds with their families and crave physical closeness. Expect Brittany to lean against your legs, curl up beside you, and generally stay within arm's reach whenever possible.

Alert: Originally bred to detect hidden game birds, Brittanys remain naturally watchful. They'll notice visitors, wildlife, and neighbourhood changes — sometimes vocally.

Versatile: Few breeds transition as seamlessly between field work and family life. The same dog that hunts tirelessly all morning will happily play with children in the afternoon.

Brittanys typically excel with children of all ages. Their medium size makes them sturdy enough to handle enthusiastic young playmates without being so large they accidentally knock toddlers over. First-time Brittany owners are often surprised by how gentle and patient these high-energy dogs become around small children.

That said, their exuberance during play means supervision is always wise, particularly with very young children who might be overwhelmed by an excited Brittany's greeting ritual.

This varies significantly between individual dogs — some Brittanys have minimal prey drive while others retain strong hunting instincts around small animals. Every Brittany is different, but early socialisation dramatically increases your chances of multi-pet harmony.

With other dogs, Brittanys are generally friendly and sociable. Their sporting background means they're accustomed to working alongside other dogs, which typically translates to good canine social skills.

If your Brittany starts becoming destructive or developing obsessive behaviours like spinning or excessive barking, insufficient exercise is almost always the culprit. Experienced handlers often say that a tired Brittany is a happy Brittany — and they're absolutely right.

Separation anxiety can affect this breed more than some others due to their strong attachment to their people. Breeders consistently note that Brittanys left alone for extended periods may develop problematic behaviours. As one Victorian breeder put it: "Brittany's idea of personal space is being in the same postcode as their favourite human — preferably the same room."

Health Issues to Know

If you're worried about health problems, you're not alone — it's one of the first things prospective owners ask. The good news is that Brittany Spaniels are generally healthy dogs with fewer inherited conditions than many purebreds, though responsible ownership means understanding the issues that can occur.

According to VCA Hospitals, hip dysplasia affects many medium-sized breeds, and They are moderately predisposed.⁴ This developmental condition causes the hip joint to form improperly, potentially leading to arthritis and pain.

  • Prevention: Buy from breeders who test parents; maintain healthy weight; appropriate exercise during growth
  • Prevalence: Approximately 14% of Brittanys tested through OFA show some degree of dysplasia⁵
  • Symptoms: Difficulty rising, reluctance to jump, bunny-hopping gait
  • Treatment Cost (AUD): $1,500 - $6,000 for surgery; ongoing management $400-1,200/year

Idiopathic epilepsy occurs in Brittanys at higher rates than the general dog population. While frightening to witness, this condition is often manageable with proper medication.

  • Management: Consistent medication, seizure tracking, regular veterinary oversight
  • Prevalence: Studies suggest elevated rates in the breed
  • Symptoms: Seizures, typically beginning between 1-5 years of age
  • Treatment Cost (AUD): $500 - $1,500 annually for medication and monitoring

Brittanys can be prone to several eye issues, including Progressive Retinal Atrophy (PRA), cataracts, and lens luxation. According to PetMD, PRA causes gradual vision loss and has no cure, making genetic testing of breeding stock essential.⁶

  • Prevention: DNA testing of breeding stock; annual eye examinations
  • Prevalence: Variable; responsible breeders screen extensively
  • Symptoms: Night blindness progressing to complete vision loss, cloudy eyes
  • Treatment Cost (AUD): $2,000 - $4,000 for cataract surgery where possible

Those beautiful floppy ears that give Brittanys their appealing expression also create a warm, moist environment where infections can thrive. Regular ear cleaning and monitoring are essential for this breed.

  • Treatment Cost (AUD): $80 - $200 per infection episode​
  • Prevention: Weekly ear checks, cleaning after swimming, keeping ears dry

Lifespan & Longevity Tips

The breed lifespan typically ranges from 12 to 14 years, which is excellent for a dog of their activity level. Many owners report their Brittanys remaining active and enthusiastic well into double digits.

To maximise your Brittany's years:

  • Maintain a lean body condition (obesity significantly impacts joint health and longevity)
  • Provide consistent mental and physical stimulation throughout life
  • Keep up with preventative veterinary care and regular health screenings
  • Address health issues early rather than waiting
  • Protect ears from chronic infections

Veterinarians at the Australian Veterinary Association recommend adjusting exercise intensity as your dog ages while maintaining activity to preserve muscle mass and mental engagement.⁷

Brittany’s Grooming Guide

The Brittany's coat is one of their more practical features — dense enough to protect them in the field, but not so heavy that it requires extensive maintenance. Their medium-length coat lies flat or slightly wavy and comes in distinctive patterns.

Do Brittany Spaniels shed? Yes, but moderately compared to many sporting breeds. You'll notice seasonal increases in shedding during spring and autumn coat changes, but daily fur tumbleweeds aren't typically a Brittany hallmark.

Grooming Schedule Table

Breed colours include orange and white, liver and white, and tricolour (liver, white, and orange). The orange and white pattern is most common, with colours ranging from pale cream to deep russet. Some Brittanys display extensive ticking (small spots of colour throughout white areas), which adds to their distinctive appearance.

Exercise Requirements

First-time Brittany owners are often surprised by just how much exercise this breed genuinely needs — and "needs" is the operative word. This is a breed developed to work all day in the field, and that stamina hasn't diminished through generations of companion breeding.

According to RSPCA Australia, sporting breeds like these dogs require substantial daily activity to maintain both physical and mental wellbeing.⁸

Minimum daily requirements:

  • 60-90 minutes of active exercise
  • Mental stimulation through training, puzzles, or scent work
  • Off-leash running opportunities several times weekly

Many Brittany owners report that their dogs thrive on closer to two hours of activity daily, particularly during their prime years (ages 2-8).

Exercise Ideas for Brittanys

  • Hiking and bushwalking (their natural environment)
  • Swimming (most Brittanys love water)
  • Fetch and retrieve games
  • Scent work and nose games
  • Agility or flyball training
  • Hunting or field trial participation

Brittanys Training Tips

This breed's intelligence and eagerness to please make them exceptionally trainable dogs. They respond beautifully to positive reinforcement and genuinely seem to enjoy the learning process. This is a breed that wants to work with you, not against you.

Don't be discouraged if your young Brittany seems easily distracted — their keen senses mean they notice everything. The good news is that with consistency and patience, they develop excellent focus and become remarkably reliable partners.

Socialisation & Training Timeline

According to the American Kennel Club, they excel in virtually every canine sport, from obedience and agility to their traditional role in field trials.⁹ If you enjoy training and want a willing, capable partner, this breed delivers.

Training Tips Specific to Brittanys:

  • Keep sessions short (10-15 minutes) and upbeat
  • Use high-value rewards — Brittanys are food and praise motivated
  • Incorporate retrieve games into training
  • Never use harsh corrections — these sensitive dogs will shut down
  • Channel their natural hunting instincts into structured activities

Price & Costs in Australia

This can feel overwhelming when you see the numbers, but being honest about costs upfront saves heartbreak later. Owning a Brittany Spaniel represents a significant financial commitment that extends well beyond the initial purchase price.

Finding Your Brittany

Find registered breeders through the Dogs Australia Breeder Directory. The breed community in Australia is relatively small but dedicated, so you may need to join waiting lists or travel interstate to find your puppy.

Consider adoption through PetRescue or sporting dog rescue organisations. While Brittanys appear in rescue less frequently than some breeds, adult dogs occasionally become available and can make wonderful companions.

Initial Costs:

Annual Ongoing Costs:

  • Quality Food: $1,000 - $1,500 (brands like Black Hawk, Advance, or Ivory Coat)
  • Vet & Preventatives: $500 - $1,000
  • Pet Insurance: $500 - $1,000
  • Grooming (supplies/occasional professional): $150 - $300
  • Training classes/activities: $200 - $600
  • Toys, treats, miscellaneous: $250 - $400
  • TOTAL ANNUAL: $2,600 - $4,800

Lifetime Cost Estimate: $38,000 - $70,000 (based on 13-year average lifespan).

Is an Australian Shepherd Right for You?

Active individuals or families who enjoy outdoor activities and can provide substantial daily exercise. You have access to safe off-leash areas, enjoy training, and want a close canine partnership. Hunters and field sport enthusiasts find natural companions in this breed.

  • Home Size: House with secure yard strongly preferred; apartments only with exceptional exercise commitment
  • Yard: Securely fenced — Brittanys are athletic and can clear surprisingly high barriers when motivated
  • Climate: Adaptable to Australian conditions; their coat provides moderate protection from both cold and heat

This can feel overwhelming, but being honest about challenges saves heartbreak later.

  • Sedentary households: If you're not genuinely active, this breed will struggle and so will you
  • Those working long hours away from home: Brittanys don't tolerate extended isolation well and may develop separation anxiety
  • People wanting a calm, quiet companion: This breed has energy to spare and will express it
  • Owners who dislike outdoor activities: Brittanys need regular access to running, exploring, and using their noses
  • Those unwilling to provide consistent training: Their intelligence requires direction, or they'll find their own entertainment

Perfect for: Active owners who want an athletic, trainable companion for outdoor adventures. Hunters seeking a versatile pointing breed. Families with children who can participate in exercise and activities. Experienced or first-time owners committed to meeting high exercise needs.

Think twice if: You prefer quiet evenings at home, work long hours away, or want a low-energy companion who's happy with brief daily walks.

First-time owner rating: Excellent choice for active first-time owners. Brittanys are forgiving of training mistakes, eager to please, and not prone to dominance challenges. Their main requirement is energy output, not experience.

The Brittany Spaniel offers a remarkable combination of athletic ability, trainability, and genuine affection that's hard to find elsewhere. They'll push you to be more active, reward your training efforts with enthusiastic progress, and greet you each day with unbridled joy. For the right owner, there's simply no better companion.

FAQs

Are Brittany Spaniels good family dogs?

Yes, They typically make excellent family dogs. Their medium size, gentle nature, and love of play make them wonderful companions for children. They're patient and affectionate without being overwhelming. The main consideration is ensuring the whole family can participate in meeting their exercise needs.

Do Brittany Spaniels shed a lot?

They are moderate shedders. You'll notice some loose hair, particularly during seasonal coat changes in spring and autumn, but they don't produce the heavy shedding associated with breeds like Golden Retrievers or German Shepherds. Weekly brushing manages loose fur effectively.¹²

How much exercise does a Brittany Spaniel need?

The average lifespan is 12-14 years with proper care. Many remain active and healthy well into their senior years. Factors that influence longevity include genetics, diet, exercise, weight management, and preventative healthcare.

How much does a puppy cost in Australia?

Expect to pay $2,000 - $4,000 for a registered puppy from a reputable breeder in Australia. Rescue adoption fees typically range from $350 - $550. Annual ownership costs run $2,600 - $4,800, meaning lifetime costs can reach $38,000 - $70,000.

Do Brittany Spaniels bark a lot?

They are moderately vocal. They'll alert you to visitors and interesting wildlife, and some individuals are more talkative than others. They're not typically excessive barkers, but they won't be silent sentinels either. Proper exercise usually reduces unnecessary barking significantly.
